microtubule buckling is a common phenomenon that can be observed in living cells.
microtubule buckling in vivo is significantly reduced by coupling to the surrounding cytoskeleton, which increases the compressive force microtubules experience and sustain.
the buckling of microtubule networks is strongly influenced by their mechanical coupling to the cytoskeleton, and that this coupling dramatically enhances the compressive loads they can sustain.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we quantitatively show how intracellular microtubes are able to resist large-scale buckling forces, and how they are able to do so by being coupled to the surrounding elastic medium.
the buckling of microtubule arrays in the cell is controlled not by their intrinsic mechanical properties, but rather by their mechanical coupling to the cytoskeleton.

the microtubule network is not only a dynamic and flexible network, but it is also able to sustain large compressive forces, and thus it can be a significant structural contributor to the mechanical behavior and shape of the cell.
The main takeaway from our work is that

microtubule buckling is not a passive consequence of compressive loads, but rather a dynamic and actively controlled response that allows microtubules to bear large compressive loads while maintaining their ability to resist tensile forces.

, while the buckling behavior of isolated microtubules is a good proxy for the behavior of individual microtubules in cells, the mechanical coupling to the cell cytoskeleton must be accounted for when considering the behavior of a population of microtubule bundles.

, while the mechanical properties of microtubule networks have been studied extensively in vitro, the in vivo mechanical properties of microfilaments and microtubules cannot be considered separately because of their intimate mechanical coupling.
